Linear Regression, Multiple Regression, and Interactions

Advanced Statistics

2025-11-25

Introduction

The fundamental equation of statistics is:

\[\text{data} = \text{model} + \text{error}\]

Our goal is to find models that minimize error while remaining interpretable and generalizable. The General Linear Model (GLM) is one of the most powerful frameworks for achieving this goal.

Key terminology:

  • Dependent variable (Y): The outcome we want to explain or predict
  • Independent variable (X): The variable(s) we use to explain Y

A general linear model expresses the dependent variable as a linear combination of independent variables, each multiplied by a weight (β):

\[\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \ldots\]

14.1 Linear Regression

Simulating the Data

Let’s create a dataset examining the relationship between study time and exam grades.

library(tidyverse)
library(broom)

# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(42)

n <- 8
study_time <- c(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4)

# Generate grades with a linear relationship + noise
# True relationship: grade = 76 + 4.3 * study_time + error
grade <- 76 + 4.3 * study_time + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 6)

df <- tibble(
  studyTime = study_time,
  grade = grade
)

# View the data
df
## # A tibble: 8 × 2
##   studyTime grade
##       <dbl> <dbl>
## 1       0.5  86.4
## 2       1    76.9
## 3       1.5  84.6
## 4       2    88.4
## 5       2.5  89.2
## 6       3    88.3
## 7       3.5 100. 
## 8       4    92.6

Visualizing the Relationship

ggplot(df, aes(x = studyTime, y = grade)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    x = "Study time (hours)",
    y = "Grade (percent)",
    title = "Relationship between Study Time and Grades"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

Correlation

Before fitting a regression model, let’s compute the correlation:

cor.test(df$grade, df$studyTime)
## 
##  Pearson's product-moment correlation
## 
## data:  df$grade and df$studyTime
## t = 2.8318, df = 6, p-value = 0.02989
## alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.1105820 0.9530545
## sample estimates:
##       cor 
## 0.7563194

The correlation tells us about the strength and direction of the linear relationship. But regression goes further—it allows us to:

  1. Describe the relationship with a specific equation
  2. Decide if the relationship is statistically significant
  3. Predict new values of Y given X

The Linear Regression Model

The simple linear regression model is:

\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \epsilon\]

Where:

  • \(\beta_1\) (slope): How much Y changes for a one-unit increase in X
  • \(\beta_0\) (intercept): The predicted value of Y when X = 0
  • \(\epsilon\) (error/residuals): What’s left over after the model fit

For prediction, we drop the error term:

\[\hat{y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x\]

Fitting the Model in R

model1 <- lm(grade ~ studyTime, data = df)
summary(model1)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = grade ~ studyTime, data = df)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -6.2966 -2.8985 -0.3898  2.1311  6.7016 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)   79.125      3.641  21.732  6.2e-07 ***
## studyTime      4.084      1.442   2.832   0.0299 *  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 4.673 on 6 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.572,  Adjusted R-squared:  0.5007 
## F-statistic: 8.019 on 1 and 6 DF,  p-value: 0.02989

Interpreting the Output

Let’s break down the key components:

  • Intercept (\(\hat{\beta}_0\)): The predicted grade when study time = 0
  • studyTime (\(\hat{\beta}_1\)): For each additional hour of study, grades increase by this amount
  • R-squared: Proportion of variance in grades explained by study time
  • F-statistic: Overall test of model significance

Visualizing the Regression Line

# Get coefficients for annotation
b0 <- coef(model1)[1]
b1 <- coef(model1)[2]

ggplot(df, aes(x = studyTime, y = grade)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Study time (hours)",
    y = "Grade (percent)",
    title = "Linear Regression: Study Time Predicting Grades",
    subtitle = paste0("Grade = ", round(b0, 1), " + ", round(b1, 2), " × Study Time")
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

Understanding R-squared

\(R^2\) tells us what fraction of the variance in Y is explained by our model:

\[R^2 = \frac{SS_{model}}{SS_{total}}\]

If the predicted values deviate from the mean in the same way the actual values do, you’ve explained a lot of variance and will result in a high \[R^2\]

If the predicted values barely move from the mean while the actual values are all over the place, you’ve explained little and will result in a low \[R^2\]

# Calculate R-squared manually
y_hat <- predict(model1)
ss_total <- sum((df$grade - mean(df$grade))^2)
ss_model <- sum((y_hat - mean(df$grade))^2)

cat("SS_total:", round(ss_total, 2), "\n")
## SS_total: 306.11
cat("SS_model:", round(ss_model, 2), "\n")
## SS_model: 175.1
cat("R-squared:", round(ss_model/ss_total, 3), "\n")
## R-squared: 0.572

14.2 Fitting More Complex Models

Adding a Categorical Predictor

What if some students had prior experience with the material? Let’s extend our dataset:

set.seed(123)

# Expanded dataset with prior class experience
df2 <- tibble(
  studyTime = c(0.5, 1, 2, 3, 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 4),
  priorClass = factor(c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1)),  # 0 = no, 1 = yes
  # Students with prior class get a boost of ~9 points
  grade = c(
    70 + 5 * 0.5 + rnorm(1, 0, 4),
    70 + 5 * 1 + rnorm(1, 0, 4),
    70 + 5 * 2 + rnorm(1, 0, 4),
    70 + 5 * 3 + rnorm(1, 0, 4),
    70 + 9 + 5 * 0.5 + rnorm(1, 0, 4),
    70 + 9 + 5 * 1.5 + rnorm(1, 0, 4),
    70 + 9 + 5 * 2.5 + rnorm(1, 0, 4),
    70 + 9 + 5 * 4 + rnorm(1, 0, 4)
  )
)

df2
## # A tibble: 8 × 3
##   studyTime priorClass grade
##       <dbl> <fct>      <dbl>
## 1       0.5 0           70.3
## 2       1   0           74.1
## 3       2   0           86.2
## 4       3   0           85.3
## 5       0.5 1           82.0
## 6       1.5 1           93.4
## 7       2.5 1           93.3
## 8       4   1           93.9

Visualizing the Two Groups

ggplot(df2, aes(x = studyTime, y = grade, color = priorClass, shape = priorClass)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("0" = "steelblue", "1" = "coral"),
                     labels = c("No prior class", "Prior class")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17),
                     labels = c("No prior class", "Prior class")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(70, 100)) +
  labs(
    x = "Study time (hours)",
    y = "Grade (percent)",
    title = "Grades by Study Time and Prior Experience",
    color = "Prior Class",
    shape = "Prior Class"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

The Multiple Regression Model

We can include both predictors:

\[\hat{y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \times \text{studyTime} + \hat{\beta}_2 \times \text{priorClass}\]

model2 <- lm(grade ~ studyTime + priorClass, data = df2)
summary(model2)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = grade ~ studyTime + priorClass, data = df2)
## 
## Residuals:
##       1       2       3       4       5       6       7       8 
## -3.9589 -2.2473  5.6891  0.5171 -1.7919  5.3320  1.0963 -4.6364 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)   72.107      3.296  21.874 3.71e-06 ***
## studyTime      4.219      1.441   2.928   0.0327 *  
## priorClass1    9.592      3.360   2.855   0.0356 *  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 4.641 on 5 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.8098, Adjusted R-squared:  0.7337 
## F-statistic: 10.64 on 2 and 5 DF,  p-value: 0.01578

Interpreting the Coefficients

  • Intercept: Predicted grade for someone with no prior class and zero study time
  • studyTime: Each additional hour increases grade by this amount (same slope for both groups)
  • priorClass1: Students with prior class score this many points higher on average

Visualizing the Parallel Lines

With an additive model (no interaction), we’re fitting parallel lines with same slope, different intercepts:

# Get coefficients
b0 <- coef(model2)[1]
b1 <- coef(model2)[2]
b2 <- coef(model2)[3]

ggplot(df2, aes(x = studyTime, y = grade, color = priorClass, shape = priorClass)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  # Line for no prior class
  geom_abline(intercept = b0, slope = b1, color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  # Line for prior class (intercept shifted by b2)
  geom_abline(intercept = b0 + b2, slope = b1, color = "coral", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("0" = "steelblue", "1" = "coral"),
                     labels = c("No prior class", "Prior class")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17),
                     labels = c("No prior class", "Prior class")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(70, 100)) +
  labs(
    x = "Study time (hours)",
    y = "Grade (percent)",
    title = "Multiple Regression",
    subtitle = paste0("Grade = ", round(b0, 1), " + ", round(b1, 2), 
                      " × StudyTime + ", round(b2, 1), " × PriorClass"),
    color = "Prior Class",
    shape = "Prior Class"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

14.3 Interactions Between Variables

A New Example: Caffeine and Public Speaking

Sometimes the effect of one variable depends on another variable. This is called an interaction.

Let’s simulate data where caffeine affects public speaking differently for anxious vs. non-anxious people:

n_per_group <- 10

# For anxious people: caffeine HURTS performance
# For non-anxious people: caffeine HELPS performance
df3 <- tibble(
  caffeine = rep(seq(10, 100, length.out = n_per_group), 2),
  anxiety = factor(rep(c("anxious", "notAnxious"), each = n_per_group)),
  speaking = c(
    # Anxious: negative slope with caffeine
    17 - 0.47 * seq(10, 100, length.out = n_per_group) + rnorm(n_per_group, 0, 8),
    # Not anxious: positive slope with caffeine  
    17 - 43 + 1.08 * seq(10, 100, length.out = n_per_group) + rnorm(n_per_group, 0, 8)
  )
)

head(df3, 12)
## # A tibble: 12 × 3
##    caffeine anxiety    speaking
##       <dbl> <fct>         <dbl>
##  1       10 anxious        6.81
##  2       20 anxious        4.03
##  3       30 anxious       12.7 
##  4       40 anxious        1.08
##  5       50 anxious       -3.29
##  6       60 anxious      -10.3 
##  7       70 anxious      -20.3 
##  8       80 anxious       -6.30
##  9       90 anxious      -21.3 
## 10      100 anxious      -45.7 
## 11       10 notAnxious    -9.59
## 12       20 notAnxious    -8.18

Ignoring Anxiety: No Apparent Effect

ggplot(df3, aes(x = caffeine, y = speaking)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "darkred") +
  labs(
    x = "Caffeine (mg)",
    y = "Public Speaking Score",
    title = "A: Caffeine and Public Speaking (Ignoring Anxiety)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

model_simple <- lm(speaking ~ caffeine, data = df3)
summary(model_simple)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = speaking ~ caffeine, data = df3)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -69.834 -15.228  -1.028  12.907  59.126 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
## (Intercept)  -5.2080    15.5314  -0.335    0.741
## caffeine      0.2931     0.2503   1.171    0.257
## 
## Residual standard error: 32.15 on 18 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.07078,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.01915 
## F-statistic: 1.371 on 1 and 18 DF,  p-value: 0.2569

No significant effect! But wait…

Visualizing by Anxiety Group

ggplot(df3, aes(x = caffeine, y = speaking, color = anxiety, shape = anxiety)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("anxious" = "tomato", "notAnxious" = "forestgreen")) +
  labs(
    x = "Caffeine (mg)",
    y = "Public Speaking Score",
    title = "B: Caffeine and Public Speaking by Anxiety Level",
    color = "Anxiety",
    shape = "Anxiety"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

Now we see a very different picture! The effect of caffeine depends on anxiety level.

Additive Model (No Interaction)

What if we add anxiety but don’t allow for an interaction?

model_additive <- lm(speaking ~ caffeine + anxiety, data = df3)
summary(model_additive)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = speaking ~ caffeine + anxiety, data = df3)
## 
## Residuals:
##    Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
## -50.65 -18.18  -1.05  15.95  39.94 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                   Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)   
## (Intercept)       -24.3899    13.6930  -1.781  0.09276 . 
## caffeine            0.2931     0.2003   1.464  0.16157   
## anxietynotAnxious  38.3637    11.5045   3.335  0.00392 **
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 25.72 on 17 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.4382, Adjusted R-squared:  0.3721 
## F-statistic: 6.631 on 2 and 17 DF,  p-value: 0.007433

Here anxiety has an effect but not caffeine, because we are forcing parallel lines when the slopes are actually opposite!

The Interaction Model

To allow different slopes for each group, we include an interaction term:

\[\hat{y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \times \text{caffeine} + \hat{\beta}_2 \times \text{anxiety} + \hat{\beta}_3 \times (\text{caffeine} \times \text{anxiety})\]

In R, we use * to include both main effects and their interaction:

model_interaction <- lm(speaking ~ caffeine * anxiety, data = df3)
summary(model_interaction)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = speaking ~ caffeine * anxiety, data = df3)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -15.1924  -4.9266  -0.0042   4.3268  14.3378 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)                 18.94976    5.41290   3.501  0.00296 ** 
## caffeine                    -0.49490    0.08724  -5.673 3.46e-05 ***
## anxietynotAnxious          -48.31560    7.65499  -6.312 1.03e-05 ***
## caffeine:anxietynotAnxious   1.57599    0.12337  12.774 8.27e-10 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 7.924 on 16 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.9498, Adjusted R-squared:  0.9404 
## F-statistic:   101 on 3 and 16 DF,  p-value: 1.308e-10

Interpreting the Interaction Model

tidy(model_interaction)
## # A tibble: 4 × 5
##   term                       estimate std.error statistic  p.value
##   <chr>                         <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
## 1 (Intercept)                  18.9      5.41        3.50 2.96e- 3
## 2 caffeine                     -0.495    0.0872     -5.67 3.46e- 5
## 3 anxietynotAnxious           -48.3      7.65       -6.31 1.03e- 5
## 4 caffeine:anxietynotAnxious    1.58     0.123      12.8  8.27e-10

Let’s unpack these coefficients:

  • Intercept (\(\hat{\beta}_0\)): Predicted speaking score for anxious people with zero caffeine
  • caffeine (\(\hat{\beta}_1\)): Slope for anxious people (caffeine hurts them)
  • anxietynotAnxious (\(\hat{\beta}_2\)): Difference in intercept for non-anxious vs. anxious
  • caffeine:anxietynotAnxious (\(\hat{\beta}_3\)): How much the slope changes for non-anxious people

For anxious people: \[\text{speaking} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \times \text{caffeine}\]

For non-anxious people: \[\text{speaking} = (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_2) + (\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_3) \times \text{caffeine}\]

Here we are fitting a different slope and a different intercept for the two group! (previously was just a different intercept)!

Visualizing the Interaction

ggplot(df3, aes(x = caffeine, y = speaking, color = anxiety, shape = anxiety)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("anxious" = "tomato", "notAnxious" = "forestgreen")) +
  labs(
    x = "Caffeine (mg)",
    y = "Public Speaking Score",
    title = "C: Interaction Model - Different Slopes by Group",
    subtitle = "Caffeine helps non-anxious speakers but hurts anxious ones",
    color = "Anxiety",
    shape = "Anxiety"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

Model Comparison

We can formally compare the additive and interaction models using ANOVA:

anova(model_additive, model_interaction)
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Model 1: speaking ~ caffeine + anxiety
## Model 2: speaking ~ caffeine * anxiety
##   Res.Df     RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
## 1     17 11250.0                                  
## 2     16  1004.6  1     10245 163.18 8.273e-10 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The significant p-value tells us the interaction model fits significantly better than the additive model.

Key Takeaways

  1. Linear regression allows us to describe, decide, and predict relationships between variables

  2. Multiple regression can include multiple predictors, including categorical variables via dummy coding

  3. Interactions are essential when the effect of one variable depends on another. Without them, we might miss important patterns or conclude there’s “no effect”

  4. Model comparison helps us determine which model best captures the structure in our data
